prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I went into the forest searching for fire inside pleading wood, but I can’t say for how long I was moored between worlds. I heard a magpie’s rumination, but I don’t know if its wings lifted the moon or let it drift slow as a little straw boat set ablaze on a winding river. I learned the yellow-eyed wolf is a dog & a man. A small boy with a star pinned to his sleeve was hiding among thorn bushes, or it was how the restless dark wounded the pale linden tree outside a Warsaw apartment. Night crawls under each stone quick as a cry held in the throat. All I remember is my left hand was holding your right breast when I forced my eyes shut. Then I could hear something in the room, magnanimous but small, half outside & half inside, no more than a song— an insomniac’s one prophecy pressed against the curtains, forcing the ferns to bloom.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Warsaw, Night, All

outputs.L1: I went into the forest in search of fire nestled within supplicant wood, though I cannot say how long I remained moored between worlds. I heard a magpie's quiet rumination, yet I could not discern whether its wings lifted the moon skyward or let it drift, slow as a little straw boat set ablaze upon a winding river. I learned that the yellow-eyed wolf is both dog and man. A small boy with a star pinned to his sleeve lay hidden among thorn bushes—or perhaps it was merely the restless dark wounding the pale linden tree outside a Warsaw apartment. Night creeps beneath every stone as swiftly as a cry held fast in the throat. All I remember is that my left hand cradled your right breast as I forced my eyes shut. Then I heard something stir within the room—magnanimous yet small, half without and half within, no more than a song: an insomniac's single prophecy pressed against the curtains, coaxing the ferns into bloom.
outputs.L2: I entered the woods in pursuit of flame trapped within suffering timber, though I couldn't tell you how long I drifted, anchored somewhere between two realities. A magpie's murmured thought reached my ears, yet whether its wingbeats carried the moon upward or released it to float gently—like a burning straw vessel upon a serpentine stream—remained uncertain to me. I discovered that the wolf with amber eyes exists as both hound and human. A boy, young and small, wore a star fastened to his sleeve while concealed among the brambles—unless this was actually the sleepless darkness inflicting harm upon the pale linden outside some Warsaw window. Beneath every stone, night creeps forward as swiftly as a stifled sob. What lingers in my memory is simply this: my left palm rested against your right breast the moment I clamped my eyes shut. Afterward, I detected a presence within the room—generous in spirit yet modest in size, existing simultaneously beyond and within, resembling nothing more than a melody—an insomniac's singular vision pressed against the drapes, coaxing the ferns into unwilling bloom.
outputs.L3:
I entered the forest the way one enters a fever—without decision, without a door. I had come searching for fire, but not the fire that lives in hearths or lanterns; I sought the fire hidden inside suffering wood, the kind that only reveals itself after the tree has already been broken, after the grain has been split and darkened by years of holding its pain quietly. Time did not pass in any way I recognized. I could not say if I had been walking for an hour or a decade. I existed suspended between two worlds, one foot in the moss and root of the visible forest, the other somewhere else entirely—in a place without geography, where only feeling had weight.

It was there that the magpie appeared, and with it, a strange uncertainty entered the night. I could not tell if the moon had been lifted quickly, snatched upward by some unseen hand, or if it had been allowed to drift, unhurried, the way a small burning straw boat drifts down a dark river, trailing embers instead of a wake. The bird's black-and-white flicker seemed to know the answer, but it offered nothing—only that sideways glint of an eye that suggested I was being watched by something older than the question itself.

Somewhere in that ambiguous light, the wolf came. Its eyes were yellow, twin lamps low to the ground, and I understood without being told that it was not simply an animal. It was dog and man at once, folded into a single shape, each nature humming beneath the other's skin like two songs sung in harmony. It did not choose between its natures; it simply was both, unresolved and whole in its unresolvedness, and I felt no fear, only recognition, as though I had always known such a creature must exist somewhere at the edge of sleep.

Then the forest gave way—or rather, folded into—another image entirely. A boy marked with a star was hiding among thorns, his small body pressed into the brambles as though the thorns themselves might protect him. But even as I saw him, I saw also the linden tree outside a Warsaw apartment, its bark torn open by some dark and violent hand, the wound in the wood bleeding shadow into the evening air. The boy and the tree became the same wound, memory and violence pressed together until I could no longer tell whether I was witnessing history or feeling it happen inside my own chest.

And then, quieter, came the memory of you. I remembered holding you close, my arms around your body in that particular intimacy that asks for nothing but presence, and I remembered forcing your eyes shut—not out of cruelty, but out of some instinct to protect you from seeing what I could not yet name. In the stillness that followed, I became aware of something small in the room with us, a presence too slight to be seen directly, ambiguous in its shape, hovering at the corner of perception. It was not until it began to sing that I understood what it was—a kind of prophecy, wordless and rising, and as its song moved through the air, the ferns in the corner of the room began to bloom, unfurling green in defiance of the season, as though the song itself carried spring inside its throat.
outputs.L4:
The path into the forest was not a path at all, but a suggestion—a parting of ferns that closed behind him as soon as he passed, as though the trees themselves were reluctant witnesses, unwilling to leave a trace of his entry. He walked without knowing whether he walked, or was carried, or simply dreamed himself forward through a green dark that thickened with each step into something older than green, older than dark.

The wolves came first, or perhaps they had always been there, grey shapes moving at the edge of sight, their eyes catching what little light filtered down through the canopy like coins at the bottom of a well. He could not tell if they hunted him or accompanied him. Their silence was not the silence of predators but of mourners, and when one lifted its head to look at him directly, he saw in its eyes not hunger but recognition, as though it had been waiting through some long winter for exactly this meeting.

Then the magpies descended—not birds now but fragments of birds, black and white scattering like torn paper, like newsprint, like the pages of ledgers no one had thought to keep. Their chattering was almost language. He caught syllables in it, names perhaps, or numbers, the kind of counting that happens in rooms with drawn curtains. They circled him in loose spirals, and each time they passed close he felt the small wind of their wings as a kind of breath against his cheek, cold and insistent.

It was in this scattering of birds that the child appeared. A boy, perhaps seven, perhaps ageless, standing very still among the birch trunks with a yellow star sewn crookedly to his coat. The star seemed to glow faintly, not with light but with the memory of light, the way a lamp glows in the mind long after the room has gone dark. The boy did not speak. He simply looked at the wanderer with eyes that held Warsaw in them—not the Warsaw of stone and steeple but the Warsaw of cellars, of held breath, of names whispered once and then never again.

The wolves, the magpies, the boy—they began to blur into one another, the grey fur and the black-white feathers and the pale small face merging as water merges when three streams meet in a single current. The wanderer could no longer say which was memory and which was myth, which had happened in some actual November and which had only ever happened in the telling, in the forest that grows up around every terrible thing to keep it from being looked at directly. He stood suspended in this blurred vision as one stands suspended in the moment before waking, when the dream has not yet released its hold and the room has not yet reasserted its walls.

And then—a touch. Not the wolves', not the birds', not even quite the boy's, but something gentler, a hand against his own, warm in a way that startled him after so much cold. He turned, though there was no one to turn to, only the sense of a presence withdrawing even as it arrived, the way sunlight touches water and is gone in the same instant it appears. The touch left something behind it: not an answer, but a permission. Permission to feel the weight he had been carrying without setting it down, permission to let the forest be what it was without demanding it resolve into simple fact or simple fable.

With the touch came the song—thin, almost nothing, a few notes strung together the way a child might hum to keep the dark at bay. He could not make out words, or perhaps there were no words, only the shape of a lullaby worn down to its skeleton, prophetic in the way that all fragile things are prophetic, hinting at what they cannot fully say. The song moved through the blurred shapes of wolf and bird and boy like a thread pulled through cloth, drawing them taut, giving them, for one moment, a single outline.

The vigilance he had carried into the forest—the old habit of watching for the wolf, the bird, the star, the habit of bracing against what memory might yield—began, note by note, to loosen its grip. Loss did not disappear; he understood it would never disappear, that it had made a home in him as permanent as bone. But it shifted, the way stone shifts almost imperceptibly under the pressure of root and season, and in the space that shifting made, he saw it: small, stubborn, absurd in its persistence—a single green shoot pushing up through the leaf-litter at his feet, curling toward whatever light found its way down through the trees.

It was not much. It was barely anything at all against the size of what the forest held. But it was alive, and it insisted on being alive, and the wanderer understood that this insistence was itself a kind of answer—not to the wolves, not to the birds, not even to the boy with his star, but to the simple fact of having entered the forest and having, somehow, still found a reason to keep walking.
outputs.L5:
# Warsaw at Night

When darkness settles over Warsaw, the city reveals a different side of itself—one that belongs to all who wander its streets after sunset. The Old Town square, rebuilt with painstaking care after the devastation of war, glows under warm lamplight, its cobblestones reflecting centuries of history alongside the footsteps of tonight's visitors.

Along the Vistula River, the city lights shimmer on the water's surface. The Palace of Culture and Science, a controversial gift from another era, stands illuminated against the night sky, visible from nearly every corner of the city—a landmark that unites the skyline regardless of one's opinion about its origins.

Warsaw's nightlife pulses with energy that welcomes all kinds of people. Praga district, once considered rough and now increasingly trendy, offers bars tucked into converted factories and courtyards where locals and travelers mix freely. Meanwhile, more polished venues near Nowy Świat cater to those seeking elegant evenings with craft cocktails and quiet conversation.

What makes Warsaw's night truly special is its accessibility to everyone. Students spill out of budget-friendly hostels to explore free walking tours under moonlight. Families stroll through illuminated parks like Łazienki, where peacocks sleep and fountains catch the light. Night owls find late-night pierogi joints serving comfort food to anyone hungry enough to wander in, whether after a concert, a long shift at work, or simply an evening of restless exploration.

The city's resilience—rebuilt from near-total destruction—feels most palpable at night, when the past and present blur together under streetlamps. All who walk through Warsaw after dark become part of its ongoing story, joining generations before them who have found something magnetic in this city once the sun goes down.

Whether you're a solo traveler, a group of friends, or someone simply passing through, Warsaw's night belongs to all.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem blending forest imagery, folklore, and wartime memory, with dreamlike shifts between fairy tale and reality.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Wolf Wears My Grandfather's Coat**

In the forest where the trees remember every name spoken beneath them, there is a path made of bread that no bird has touched in eighty years. I follow it anyway, the way you follow a story you already know will end badly, because the ending is not the point—the walking is the point, the going-toward is the point.

My grandmother told me once that during the war, the wolves came down from the hills and slept beside the soldiers because everyone was equally hungry, equally far from home. I did not believe her. I believed her completely. Both things were true the way fairy tales are true, which is to say: not literally, but in the bones.

The witch's house here is made of ration cards instead of gingerbread. The windows are blackout curtains that never lift. When I press my ear to the door I hear my grandfather's voice reciting the names of villages that no longer appear on any map, villages swallowed by forest the way the forest swallows all abandoned things—slowly, patiently, with great tenderness, the way a wolf swallows a grandmother and later regurgitates her whole, unharmed, wearing a different face.

I am both the child lost in these trees and the child who was told about these trees by someone lost in them first. Time folds like a paper crane, like a letter never sent, like the collapsible boats we made from newsprint headlines: SIEGE, LIBERATION, ARMISTICE, folded until the words became wings, became small enough to drown in a puddle, in a helmet filling with rain.

Somewhere in this forest, my grandfather is nineteen and running. Somewhere he is ninety and forgetting. Somewhere he is neither, is only breath caught between two trees that used to be soldiers, or soldiers that used to be trees—I can no longer tell where the transformation happened, only that it did, the way all transformations happen: overnight, in silence, without permission.

The wolf wearing my grandfather's coat asks me riddles I cannot answer. *What grows in the space where a house used to stand? What blooms from a helmet left in a field? What song does the forest sing when there is no one left to hear it, and does it sing it anyway?*

I tell him I don't know. I tell him this is not that kind of story.

But he only smiles with my grandfather's mouth, and the trees lean in closer, and the path made of bread begins, very slowly, to disappear behind me—each crumb lifting into the dark like something small and finally, mercifully, allowed to fly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a piece of poetic flash fiction that mixes magical realism with a hidden Holocaust narrative, using ambiguous, shifting imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Cartographer of Absent Streets

Grandmother kept a map of the old city folded into her sleeve, and when she thought no one watched, she would trace her finger along streets that no longer existed, or existed only as she remembered them—crooked, cobbled, humming with a language that tasted of rain and yeast.

"Here," she'd whisper, "the baker sold bread shaped like birds. They would fly away if you didn't eat them fast enough."

I never believed the birds were bread. I never believed the bread was birds either. Both truths lived in her mouth like stones she'd swallowed and couldn't cough up.

The map changed each time she opened it. Sometimes the river ran red with autumn leaves. Sometimes there was no river at all, just a long gray absence where water used to argue with its banks. She said the city breathed—inhaled its people in winter, exhaled them in spring, though some springs never came, some winters lasted forty years in a single night.

I asked her once why the map had no names on the buildings.

"Names," she said, "are the first things that learn to fly. Then windows. Then doors. Then—" She stopped. Her finger hovered over a blank space where, I would later understand, a synagogue had folded itself into smoke and rearranged its molecules into something the wind could carry.

The birds came back every Yom Kippur, gray-winged, silent, landing on her windowsill like paper made flesh. She fed them crumbs from bread she baked herself, dark and dense, nothing like the birds from her stories. I asked if these were the same birds.

"No," she said. "Yes." She looked at me the way you'd look at a door that used to be a wall. "They are the grandchildren of birds. They don't remember flying from the ovens. They only remember that their grandmothers taught them the shape of leaving."

The last time I saw the map, it had become entirely blank—not empty, but *waiting*, the way a throat is waiting before a scream, the way silence is waiting before it becomes a name again. She folded it back into her sleeve and it disappeared, the way certain streets disappear, the way six million shapes can fold themselves into the sleeve of a single grandmother, into the single word *remember*, which she said the way you'd say a location, a coordinate, a birdless sky where something once, impossibly, could fly.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness prose poem about a man wandering between fantasy and memory, incorporating symbols like a magpie, a wolf, and a boy with a star on his sleeve.
counterfactuals.output:
He walks and the road keeps forgetting itself behind him, gravel to grass to the long silver hush of a field he swears he's seen before, maybe in a dream, maybe on a Tuesday thirty years gone, and there — always there — the magpie lands on the fence post like a black-and-white punctuation mark, one for sorrow, isn't that what the old rhyme says, one for sorrow and he counts and there is only one, always only one, watching him with that oil-slick eye that holds the whole sky bent small inside it.

He is a boy again for a moment. He is a man walking. He is both, the seams show, the light comes through the seams.

There was a boy with a star sewn crooked on his sleeve — his brother, was it, or himself, or someone borrowed from a story told too many times by a fire that has long since gone to ash and then to nothing, not even smoke, not even the memory of smoke — and that boy ran ahead through wheat that came up to his shoulders, laughing in a way that doesn't survive translation into adult language, and the star on his sleeve caught what light there was and threw it back changed, softer, like a coin passed through so many hands it becomes warm rather than metal.

Somewhere behind the wheat, or after it, or wearing it like a coat, is the wolf. It has always been there. It is not chasing so much as accompanying, the way grief accompanies, the way a name you no longer say aloud still walks beside you shaped like an animal because animals don't ask you to explain yourself. The wolf's eyes are amber the way the last hour before dark is amber. The wolf does not want to eat him. The wolf wants him to remember something he agreed to forget.

The magpie again, further on, or the same magpie, unkillable, immortal in the way small thieving birds are immortal, carrying in its beak something bright it stole from a life he used to have — a button, a coin, a fragment of a wedding ring, a word his mother said once and never again — and he wants it back, he reaches, the bird lifts three feet and no more, always three feet and no more, keeping the distance of memory, which is close enough to break your heart and far enough to never let you touch it.

He is walking through the field and he is walking through the house he grew up in and he is walking through the hospital corridor with its particular green quiet and he is walking through none of these because his feet have stopped somewhere and only his mind goes on, wandering the way water wanders down a hill, taking the shape of whatever it moves through.

The boy with the star is calling him from ahead, or is it from before, language fails at the tense of it, come on, come on, as if there is a place to arrive at, as if arrival were still a thing that could happen to a man his age, in his condition, with a wolf for a shadow and a thief for a compass.

And the wolf says nothing because wolves in dreams and memories never need to, its silence is the whole of what it has to say, and the magpie chatters its two-note nonsense which might be laughter or might be the only kind of prayer birds are permitted, and the star on the boy's sleeve is not a badge, he understands now, walking, always walking, it is a wound that healed wrong and beautifully, the way all the best of us heal, wrong and beautiful and shining a little too much in the dark.

He does not know if he is going toward something or away, only that the field does not end, that the light is the amber of the wolf's eye and the black-white flicker of the bird and the small distant star-shaped brightness of the boy who may be him, who may be gone, who may be the one thing he has been walking toward this entire time without ever admitting that walking was the same thing as searching, and searching the same thing as grief, and grief the same thing, in the end, as love that has nowhere left to be delivered.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a lyrical, dreamlike paragraph that merges eroticism, folklore, and historical trauma (like Warsaw during WWII) in an abstract, non-linear way.
counterfactuals.output: In the cellars beneath Warsaw's breathing rubble, she undresses like a rumor, her spine an alphabet of ash and honey. The old wives said: when the city burns twice, love learns to walk backward through smoke. His hands remember her before they touch her—hands that once held bread that wasn't bread, that held names that became numbers, that held nothing and called it prayer. She is the fox-bride from the forest tales, the one who marries the soldier and the soldier is already dead and already alive, stitched together by curfew and moonlight. Skin against skin against the memory of a wall that stood where laughter used to. The river Vistula carries their voices downstream to 1943, to a bed made of newspaper and static, where desire is just another word for what the war didn't finish eating. Somewhere a grandmother spins straw into names for children who will not be born, while somewhere else, in the same somewhere, two mouths find each other in the dark like the last unburned page of a book everyone was forced to memorize. This is how the dead learn to be tender—through the living, who fuck like they're translating grief into a language with no future tense, only the eternal aching now of ruins that keep blooming, obscene and holy, into morning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short surrealist narrative in a poetic voice, filled with animal transformations, insomnia, and blurred boundaries between love and violence.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Night Keeps

I have not slept since the fox climbed out of my mouth wearing my mother's voice.

This is how it begins: the ceiling turns to water, and I float there, face-up, counting the wings that gather like debt in the corners. My lover sleeps beside me in the shape of something I no longer recognize—antlers pushing through the pillow, breath rattling like a hive disturbed. I touch what was his shoulder. It gives like wet paper. Underneath: feathers, or scales, or the memory of hands.

*Love me anyway*, says the mouth that used to be his mouth.

The hours do not pass so much as molt. I shed the version of myself that could close her eyes. In the mirror, my teeth have gone soft and many, small as a shrew's, arranged for a different kind of hunger. I bite down on nothing and taste copper, taste the color of wanting something to hurt you gently.

Outside, dogs are turning into weather. I hear them change—the low growl becoming thunder, becoming the sound a door makes when it decides, finally, not to be a door. I have loved like that: all threshold, no room. I have loved like a trap that mistakes itself for a nest.

The fox is back in my throat, curled around my hesitation. It whispers with my mother's patience: *pain is just love that forgot its own name.* I want to disagree. I want to sleep. Instead I watch my lover's hand become a wing become a fist become a hand again, tender, terrible, reaching for me in the dark like it isn't sure whether to hold me or take back everything it gave.

Somewhere, a clock is trying to be a heartbeat.

I let it.

I stay awake to witness the shapes love takes when no one is measuring the damage—the way tenderness curls its fingers into claws just to feel how sharp it could have been, the way a bite can be a kind of prayer if you say it soft enough.

By morning I am covered in fur that isn't mine, in a bed that keeps forgetting its shape, beside a body still deciding what it loves enough to become.

I do not sleep.

I molt instead, endlessly, into whoever will hold me next—fox-mouthed, wing-boned, awake as a wound that has learned to call itself a window.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
